power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Existential Psychotherapy and the Human Condition: Philosophical Foundations, Clinical Practice, and the Challenge of Evidence

text.text: Existential psychotherapy addresses suffering from a position that resists reduction to pathology: confrontations with death, freedom, isolation, and meaninglessness that manualized frameworks tend to bracket.

Despite its prominent influence on the history and development of psychotherapies, the existential tradition has lost ground in a field characterized by symptom reduction and reimbursable outcomes, in part due to a thin empirical foundation and resistance to structured approaches.

This thematic review traces existential therapy from its philosophical foundations in phenomenology and existentialism, through core models of Frankl, Yalom, and May, to more contemporary integrative and meaning-centered approaches.

Across process, qualitative, and outcome research, three commitments recur: meaning as a mechanism of recovery, therapeutic relationship as the site of change, and clients' authority over their experience.
Meta-analytic evidence indicates that meaning-centered interventions increase meaning and reduce distress.
Therapeutic realness is generally associated with stronger client alliances, while existential-humanistic principles play an integral role in effective psychotherapy broadly.

Existential therapies are not irrelevant, but lack infrastructure: measurement of proposed mechanisms, methods to identify target populations, and training guidelines that prepare therapists to meet existential encounters.
Precision-based methods offer a promising path toward an existential therapy that is empirically legible while true to its core commitments.
Psychotherapeutic modalities are typically defined by their techniques and by theoretical assumptions about what causes distress and which principles effect change (Anderson et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Psychotherapeutic modalities are typically defined by their techniques and by theoretical assumptions about what causes distress and which principles effect change <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anderson et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Yet outcomes depend substantially on how those techniques are delivered (Hill, 2005), and factors such as therapeutic alliance and client-therapist fit contribute to outcomes, often beyond the modality itself (Norcross & Wampold, 2011).
text.formatted: Yet outcomes depend substantially on how those techniques are delivered <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hill, 2005)</ref>, and factors such as therapeutic alliance and client-therapist fit contribute to outcomes, often beyond the modality itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Norcross & Wampold, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Fidelity to the modality, client expectations, relational patterns between client and therapist, and various external factors all shape the therapeutic process (Sousa, 2015).
text.formatted: Fidelity to the modality, client expectations, relational patterns between client and therapist, and various external factors all shape the therapeutic process <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Sousa, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: If so much of what heals lies outside technique, in the persons and the relationship between them, then a tradition that places both at its center deserves renewed attention.
Existential psychotherapy occupies a strange position across modality, philosophy, and technique.

Loosely defined, it is a modality that emphasizes the confrontation of existential givens (e.g., death, anxiety, dread) through a shared journey with the therapist using genuine and non-judgmental guidance.

However, existentialism can also complement rather than replace other modalities (Leontiev, 2015), or stand wholly unattached to modality and technique as a philosophical facilitation of the therapeutic approach.
text.formatted: However, existentialism can also complement rather than replace other modalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Leontiev, 2015)</ref>, or stand wholly unattached to modality and technique as a philosophical facilitation of the therapeutic approach.

text.text: Overall, existentialism attempts to come to terms with the absurdity of life's suffering without pathologizing the strain that takes place (Berra, 2021).
text.formatted: Overall, existentialism attempts to come to terms with the absurdity of life's suffering without pathologizing the strain that takes place <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Berra, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: While the questions of existence (death, freedom, isolation) are necessarily unanswerable, restitution is found in a direction, purpose, or meaning (Berra, 2021).
text.formatted: While the questions of existence (death, freedom, isolation) are necessarily unanswerable, restitution is found in a direction, purpose, or meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Berra, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Attempts have been made to reintroduce existential initiatives into contemporary psychotherapy, but its role is best demonstrated by what the field lacks.
A common practice of psychotherapy is the pathologizing of psychological processes.
Impaired insight (e.g., psychosis), for instance, is not necessarily psychological in its origin (Ghaemi, 2007).
text.formatted: Impaired insight (e.g., psychosis), for instance, is not necessarily psychological in its origin <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Ghaemi, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The separation of abnormal from normal psychology, an "us" and "them," was considered dismantled when phenomenology had prominent influence over psychotherapy (Wharne, 2021), yet contemporary psychotherapy still adheres to it.
text.formatted: The separation of abnormal from normal psychology, an "us" and "them," was considered dismantled when phenomenology had prominent influence over psychotherapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Wharne, 2021)</ref>, yet contemporary psychotherapy still adheres to it.

text.text: The humanness surrounding the temporal experience of depression and anxiety is not fully met by addressing psychopathology alone (Rayner & Vitali, 2016), which can leave psychotherapy vulnerable to medical reductionism.
text.formatted: The humanness surrounding the temporal experience of depression and anxiety is not fully met by addressing psychopathology alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Rayner & Vitali, 2016)</ref>, which can leave psychotherapy vulnerable to medical reductionism.

text.text: In an age of manualized reimbursement and coverage, a clinic's ability to function is contingent on demonstrating symptom reduction (Bland, 2025).
text.formatted: In an age of manualized reimbursement and coverage, a clinic's ability to function is contingent on demonstrating symptom reduction <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bland, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: When demonstrated progress is required, it can be difficult to incorporate a client's meaning-making or self-motivation (Wharne, 2021).
text.formatted: When demonstrated progress is required, it can be difficult to incorporate a client's meaning-making or self-motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Wharne, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This reflects what Leontiev (2005) summarizes as the assumption of classical psychology: that human behavior can be determined in a predictable fashion, provided all relevant factors are considered.
text.formatted: This reflects what <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Leontiev (2005)</ref> summarizes as the assumption of classical psychology: that human behavior can be determined in a predictable fashion, provided all relevant factors are considered.

text.text: The same assumption underlies the widespread reliance on the GAD and PHQ for substantiating a modality's progress and effectiveness.
Moreover, the clinical efficacy of a therapeutic research trial is often not reflected in the clinical effectiveness of routine therapy (Rainer & Gay, 2013).
text.formatted: Moreover, the clinical efficacy of a therapeutic research trial is often not reflected in the clinical effectiveness of routine therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Rainer & Gay, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: While contemporary psychotherapy is equipped to take on certain levels of psychological distress and maladjustment, true crises present a roadblock.

Personal crises, which may be understood as existential, do not respond well to classical approaches because the situation does not allow for a productive way to achieve therapeutic goals (Leontiev, 2005).
text.formatted: Personal crises, which may be understood as existential, do not respond well to classical approaches because the situation does not allow for a productive way to achieve therapeutic goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Leontiev, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Clinicians, especially those who work with young persons, also hesitate to adopt existential approaches because of the relative lack of empirical evidence and concrete treatment guidelines (Keshen, 2006; Schneider, 2008).
text.formatted: Clinicians, especially those who work with young persons, also hesitate to adopt existential approaches because of the relative lack of empirical evidence and concrete treatment guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Keshen, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Schneider, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: When 26 trained psychotherapists watched a recorded session of a client overwhelmed by meaninglessness and were asked to imagine themselves as the client's therapist, the majority described withdrawing from the therapeutic encounter (Vanhees, 2021, as cited in Vanhooren, 2022).
text.formatted: When 26 trained psychotherapists watched a recorded session of a client overwhelmed by meaninglessness and were asked to imagine themselves as the client's therapist, the majority described withdrawing from the therapeutic encounter (Vanhees, 2021, as cited in <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Vanhooren, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Even so, writing on existential training focuses on the relational process of supervision rather than extending existential philosophy into practice (Smith et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Even so, writing on existential training focuses on the relational process of supervision rather than extending existential philosophy into practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Smith et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Despite its loss of influence in contemporary psychotherapy, existential practice still holds potential and importance.
This paper is a thematic review that traces the philosophical and clinical foundations of existentialism into the meaning-centered approaches now gaining empirical support.

It seeks to contextualize what existential approaches have inherited, what they risk leaving behind, and what an empirically engaged existentialism would need to retain to remain both faithful to its commitments and mindful of its limits.
Existential psychotherapy builds upon depth psychology and existential philosophy, a mode of inquiry into the human confrontation with existential givens (death, anxiety, grief, etc.).
For Heidegger, the state of Being is inherently tied to the being in which it is experienced (Heidegger, 1927 (Heidegger, /2001, p. 33), p. 33).
text.formatted: For Heidegger, the state of Being is inherently tied to the being in which it is experienced <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Heidegger, 1927</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Heidegger, /2001, p. 33), p. 33)</ref>.

text.text: For Camus, to understand the world is to reduce it to human terms, stamping it with a human seal; yet the world resists this demand for clarity, and the absurd arises from their confrontation (Camus, 1942 (Camus, /1991, pp. 9-10), pp. 9-10).
text.formatted: For Camus, to understand the world is to reduce it to human terms, stamping it with a human seal; yet the world resists this demand for clarity, and the absurd arises from their confrontation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Camus, 1942</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Camus, /1991, pp. 9-10), pp. 9-10)</ref>.

text.text: Truth, for Heidegger, is only secondarily the agreement of a statement with its object; primarily, it is the disclosedness of Being itself (Heidegger, 1927 (Heidegger, /2001, p. 62), p. 62).
text.formatted: Truth, for Heidegger, is only secondarily the agreement of a statement with its object; primarily, it is the disclosedness of Being itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Heidegger, 1927</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Heidegger, /2001, p. 62), p. 62)</ref>.

text.text: Existential phenomenology thus holds that Being and truth cannot be understood outside the existing individual through whom they are disclosed.

For Kierkegaard, the deepest commitments cannot be reached by reason alone; in Fear and Trembling, Abraham's faith is a leap made by the individual, held by virtue of the absurd rather than secured by argument (Kierkegaard, 1843 (Kierkegaard, /2000)).
text.formatted: For Kierkegaard, the deepest commitments cannot be reached by reason alone; in Fear and Trembling, Abraham's faith is a leap made by the individual, held by virtue of the absurd rather than secured by argument <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kierkegaard, 1843</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kierkegaard, /2000))</ref>.

text.text: Existentialism inherits this: a meaningful life is pursued without guarantee, in the face of uncertainty and death.

For Tillich, courage is the self-affirmation of being in spite of nonbeing, holding these ultimate threats together in a meaningful present rather than escaping them (Tillich, 1952 (Tillich, /2000, pp. 152-153), pp. 152-153).
text.formatted: For Tillich, courage is the self-affirmation of being in spite of nonbeing, holding these ultimate threats together in a meaningful present rather than escaping them <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Tillich, 1952</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Tillich, /2000, pp. 152-153), pp. 152-153)</ref>.

text.text: Nihilism presses the opposite case.

Schopenhauer positions vanity squarely: that which wastes away cannot be worth any straining effort (Schopenhauer, 1851 (Schopenhauer, /2004, p. 52), p. 52), and nihilism arises when the self has become disillusioned with all meaning (Nietzsche, 1901 (Nietzsche, /2017, p. 18), p. 18).
text.formatted: Schopenhauer positions vanity squarely: that which wastes away cannot be worth any straining effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Schopenhauer, 1851</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Schopenhauer, /2004, p. 52), p. 52)</ref>, and nihilism arises when the self has become disillusioned with all meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Nietzsche, 1901</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Nietzsche, /2017, p. 18), p. 18)</ref>.

text.text: Existentialism does not seek to answer whether ultimate purpose exists, but how to strive forward while death, anxiety, and adversity linger on.
The self has the freedom to choose their course of action, and with that freedom comes the responsibility to act in a manner that reflects all humanity (Sartre, 1946 (Sartre, /2007, p. 29), p. 29).
text.formatted: The self has the freedom to choose their course of action, and with that freedom comes the responsibility to act in a manner that reflects all humanity <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Sartre, 1946</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Sartre, /2007, p. 29), p. 29)</ref>.

text.text: For Sartre, because existence precedes essence, individuals are not bound by predetermination; rather, they exert themselves through their choices and actions.
Existential inquiry consequently begins with the subjective experience of being in such a world.

Levinas extends this as a responsibility beyond the self: no other can assume one's responsibility for the Other, and ethical existence requires seeking the same freedom for others as one does the self (Levinas, 1974 (Levinas, /1981, p. 141), p. 141).
text.formatted: Levinas extends this as a responsibility beyond the self: no other can assume one's responsibility for the Other, and ethical existence requires seeking the same freedom for others as one does the self <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Levinas, 1974</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Levinas, /1981, p. 141), p. 141)</ref>.

text.text: Existentialism positions itself as an acknowledgement of the fundamental and harsh givens of life and the responsibility to recognize the freedom and subjectivity of others.
Viktor Frankl's existential approach arises from the confrontation with adversity.
Suffering is a given in this world; perhaps it was not a chosen life, but it is life nonetheless.

Frankl holds to this even in an event as catastrophic as the Holocaust, reaffirming that a life in suffering remains a meaningful pursuit: it is the realization of meaning that allows suffering to cease being suffering (Frankl, 1963, p. 122).
text.formatted: Frankl holds to this even in an event as catastrophic as the Holocaust, reaffirming that a life in suffering remains a meaningful pursuit: it is the realization of meaning that allows suffering to cease being suffering <ref type="bibr">(Frankl, 1963, p. 122)</ref>.

text.text: Responsibility for finding that meaning is, in part, other-sparing.
With the death of a loved one, the suffering felt in grief is also the opportunity to have spared that loved one the suffering of one's own death (Frankl, 1963, p. 172).
text.formatted: With the death of a loved one, the suffering felt in grief is also the opportunity to have spared that loved one the suffering of one's own death <ref type="bibr">(Frankl, 1963, p. 172)</ref>.

text.text: For the therapist, trust in being not only allows fortitude in challenges, but allows the session to be void of ideological stance (Frankl, 1967).
text.formatted: For the therapist, trust in being not only allows fortitude in challenges, but allows the session to be void of ideological stance <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Frankl, 1967)</ref>.

text.text: Irvin Yalom, who laid the groundwork for group therapy and other modern existential approaches, proposes that the essence of being is the confrontation of four existential themes: death, freedom, isolation, and meaninglessness (Yalom, 1980, pp. 481-482).

text.text: The goal of existential psychotherapy is not to eliminate it, but to balance the fear of death with the essence of living; as Tillich writes, the threat of nonbeing can never be erased, only met with courage (Tillich, 1952 (Tillich, /2000, p. 39), p. 39).

text.text: Grounding, for Yalom, is the mandate to live truthfully, balancing Schopenhauer's awareness of oblivion with Nietzsche's gay science.
Importantly, Yalom does not contend that the absence of meaning causes psychopathology: diminished meaning in life is a common co-occurrence (Yalom, 1980, p. 460).

text.text: A central premise of existential psychotherapy is that the client's autonomy and being should be respected.

The client-therapist relationship hinges on the ability to sit on level ground, to walk a path together for some time, and to recognize when the relationship would not be beneficial (Perls, 1969, p. 4).

text.text: What further separates existential psychotherapy from psychoanalysis is the acknowledgment of the creative will, a life-affirming forward direction that Otto Rank held to be better understood through phenomenology and a perspective-taking of the other (Rank, 1936 (Rank, /1978)).

text.text: It also asks that the therapist be able to take on the pain, grief, and suffering of another person without losing one's self (Rogers, 1980, pp. 142-143).

text.text: Across the decades, existential psychotherapy has preserved its core goal: reorienting an otherwise meaningless, limited being toward a purposeful way forward.

Changing one's orientation to meaning and ordering of values requires the balancing of two truths, a yin and yang (Rayner & Vitali, 2018): humans seek a meaningful life in an otherwise meaningless and cruel reality.
text.formatted: Changing one's orientation to meaning and ordering of values requires the balancing of two truths, a yin and yang <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Rayner & Vitali, 2018)</ref>: humans seek a meaningful life in an otherwise meaningless and cruel reality.

text.text: This encounter with meaning is inevitable.

Clients and clinicians alike may not put a name to it, but the exploration of thoughts and feelings to gain clarity and coherence and to deepen one's sense of self is an encounter with meaning in life (Hill, 2017).
text.formatted: Clients and clinicians alike may not put a name to it, but the exploration of thoughts and feelings to gain clarity and coherence and to deepen one's sense of self is an encounter with meaning in life <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hill, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: To this degree, existential meaning is present in all therapeutic encounters.

Where empiricism often treats behavior and cognition in terms of their divergence from a normative threshold, phenomenology treats subjective experience as a fundamental cue into the patient's state and being, contextualized by personal variance and history.
Both are useful: one asks how far a person departs from the norm, the other whether that departure is understandable given the circumstances.
Just as a mild depressive state was once filtered solely through psychoanalysis, modern protocols may unnecessarily filter it through CBT (Ghaemi, 2007).

text.text: With Dostoevsky's underground man, an existential approach would not medicalize the internal rage, but contextualize it as unrelinquished existential distress and an attempt at meaning-making (Aho, 2021).

text.text: Existential psychotherapy was unique for its time in the emphasis it placed on the therapist-client coupling.

The APA task force on evidence-based therapy relationships concluded that the relationship contributes to outcome consistently and independently of treatment type, and that tailoring it to what each client brings (e.g., culture, preferences, history) enhances effectiveness (Norcross & Wampold, 2011).

text.text: This path is demanding.

Attending equally and deeply to every dimension of a client's experience would likely overwhelm most novice therapists (Sotskova & Dossett, 2017), and the experiential nature of the training entails a period of profound anxiety and uncertainty (Smith et al., 2023).

text.text: The purpose of an existential approach is therefore not to change or rebuild the inner world of the client, much less to get rid of that which humans are in essence (Kociunas, 2007), but to help the individual find their own way through the world, drawing on the creative will and intention (Ratner, 2019).

text.text: Existential therapy is also integrative in nature.

It emphasizes a holistic understanding of the client, seeking to simultaneously address cognition, affect, behavior, and relational facets while holding close the idea of a deeply meaningful being (Sotskova et al., 2016).
text.formatted: It emphasizes a holistic understanding of the client, seeking to simultaneously address cognition, affect, behavior, and relational facets while holding close the idea of a deeply meaningful being <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Sotskova et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In a controlled merging of life-worlds, the joint interaction with an ambivalent Other allows for the transformation of the inner self (Krasilnikov, 2022).
text.formatted: In a controlled merging of life-worlds, the joint interaction with an ambivalent Other allows for the transformation of the inner self <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Krasilnikov, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Existential phenomenology seeks to treat not symptoms in isolation, but the whole of every unique situation in which we are found, affectively and relationally (Aho, 2021).

text.text: Existential psychotherapy differentiates its approach from other modalities in that gathering information begins from the old Socratic saying, "I know that I know nothing" (Rayner & Vitali, 2018).

text.text: The position of knowing, describing, or changing is consequently in the hands of the patient: change is effected by facilitating discovery, not by preconceived notions and general training (Berra, 2021; Rayner & Vitali, 2018).

text.text: Therapy does not presuppose that mental suffering must be classified as a pathology or that outcomes are the only measure of interest (Berra, 2021; Bland, 2025), and it encourages epistemological pluralism and eclectic training while cautioning against scientism's exclusivity (DeRobertis & Bland, 2025).

text.text: Lastly, the existential framework is characterized by the relationship of patient and therapist, in which themes of freedom, responsibility, and finite limitation allow authentic self-disclosure and genuine concern (Krasilnikov, 2022; Sotskova & Dossett, 2017).

text.text: Existential therapy is particularly well equipped to address suffering not easily situated in standard diagnostic categories. Berra (2021) describes an existential depression rooted not in cognitive distortion but in an overtly accurate, and therefore unbearable, confrontation with the tragic facets of existence.

text.text: Current classifications tend to fold this state into the same diagnostic criteria and treatment plan as other depressive categories, heightening the risk of an inappropriate protocol.
Existential work also offers an alternative to the struggle-against model of distress.
As Rainer and Gay (2013) note, efforts to overpower unwanted internal experience tend to intensify its negative consequences.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Rainer and Gay (2013)</ref> note, efforts to overpower unwanted internal experience tend to intensify its negative consequences.

text.text: Existential and acceptance-based approaches instead give the client a platform to stop fighting and reorient toward what they perceive as mattering.

Clients who have received existential therapy describe a greater capacity to cope with specific areas of life and their relationships, and a newly sparked sense of what their lives could be (Sousa & Vaz, 2020).
text.formatted: Clients who have received existential therapy describe a greater capacity to cope with specific areas of life and their relationships, and a newly sparked sense of what their lives could be <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Sousa & Vaz, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The distress existential therapy addresses most directly takes the form of Yalom's (1980) ultimate concerns as they appear in lived experience. Berra (2017) characterizes it as a diffuse anguish that follows the loss of reference points, the sense that the frame by which one had oriented one's life no longer holds.

text.text: Its defining feature is hopelessness in a specific sense: the existential depressive can no longer deny the tragedy of life that others have kept at a distance (Berra, 2021).

text.text: The therapeutic response is not resignation.
Acceptance, better understood as willingness, is an active openness to one's situation and being (Rainer & Gay, 2013).

text.text: Meaning-centered suffering is therefore addressed not by supplying answers but by accompanying the client as they reconstruct a livable orientation to their own life.

Qualitative and Case-Based Support While existentialism has historically been hesitant to take on empirical backing, recent research has begun classifying and measuring the outcomes of existential programs.
Qualitative research offers perhaps the most direct view of what clients and therapists experience as effective.

Across two sets of Belgian person-centered case studies (43 and 42 cases, each spanning 15 or more sessions), all four of Yalom's concerns appeared in every case (De Decker, 2020, and Helsen, 2020, as cited in Vanhooren, 2022).

text.text: However, the weight given to existential material differs considerably.

Group therapists in correctional settings ranked existential factors tenth of Yalom's eleven therapeutic factors (Morgan et al., 1999), whereas a sample of offenders ranked them second (MacDevitt & Sanislow, 1987).

text.text: Clients' own accounts emphasize both relational and personal change.

They attribute significant moments partly to the therapist's skill, but also to their own reflective effort and to being recognized and validated in their sense of being by another; they describe recovering a sense of purpose, a clearer identity, greater acceptance of previously rejected parts of themselves, and a maturation that sits side-by-side with a better quality of life (Sousa & Vaz, 2020).

Adolescents think about existential questions and can process them with at least some sophistication (Berman et al., 2006 (Berman et al., , 2009)).

Quantitative outcome research, albeit more recent, has begun to support these accounts.

Across hundreds of studies, the presence of meaning and meaning-oriented coping have been moderately to strongly associated with higher quality of life, lower depression and anxiety, and better physical health (Vos, 2023).

text.text: A later meta-analysis extends these findings.
From pre-treatment, clients improved substantially in quality of life (g = 1.13 post-treatment; g = 0.99 at follow-up) and psychological stress (g = 1.21; g = 0.67).

In controlled trials, large advantages over control conditions survived for both quality of life (g = 1.02; g = 1.06) and psychological stress (g = 0.94; g = 0.84), and did not differ meaningfully by sample type or method of study selection.
Most interestingly, increases in meaning predicted decreases in psychological stress (β = -0.56; & Vitali, 2018).

text.text: Because this is a study-level meta-regression, it is an ecological association between studies rather than evidence that a given client's distress falls as their meaning rises, a distinction taken up in the methods proposed below.

Evidence from routine care is also encouraging. Rayner and Vitali (2016) delivered a sixsession intervention in UK primary care to clients referred for mild-to-moderate depression or anxiety, with large pre-post reductions in depressive symptoms (PHQ-9, d_z = 1.38), anxiety (GAD-7, d_z = 1.09), and general distress (CORE-OM, d_z = 0.89).

text.text: These effects come from a non-controlled design, which leaves them prone to regression to the mean and non-specific effects; they speak less to efficacy than to feasibility and acceptability in a service context.
Existential theory holds that the relationship itself is the vehicle of change, and process research lends partial support.

Therapeutic realness, the therapist's willingness to share genuine thoughts and feelings at some personal risk, is more frequent in process-oriented than in cognitive-behavioral treatments and is associated with stronger real relationships, working alliances, and therapeutic presence (Hopwood et al., 2024).

text.text: Existential therapists describe this authenticity as a way to keep patients oriented to the process of their experience rather than piling up content (Rayner & Vitali, 2018).

text.text: Authenticity here has a precise meaning, a sense of authorship: an action is authentic when chosen and held with full awareness of the situation and its consequences (Van Deurzen & Adams, 2011).

text.text: As they succinctly describe, "authentic living is aware living" (p. 92).
If existential therapy asks therapists to apply its ideas to their own lives, it also changes them.

Therapists who regularly engage with clients' existential concerns report becoming more aware of their own existential reality, adjusting their lives, tolerating more presence with clients' concerns, and developing more nuanced views of life's central questions; those with existential training more often picked up implicit and complex existential dynamics than those without it (Frediani et al., 2023).

text.text: Existential therapy shares more with contemporary approaches than its reputation may suggest.

Beck and colleagues explicitly credit the phenomenological movement, rooted in Kant, Heidegger, and Husserl, and its clinical application by Jaspers, Binswanger, and Straus, as influences on cognitive therapy (Beck et al., 1979, p. 9).

text.text: This is apparent in the focus on what is directly accessible to the therapist, rather than the therapist acting as interpreter, and in the cognitive triad of self, world, and future (Menzies et al., 2023). Rainer and Gay (2013) likewise map the bridges between existential therapy and ACT onto three levels: content, where the client's problems are met with nonjudgmental observation; processing, where attention shifts to the strategies the client uses to meet a problem's demands; and relationship, treated throughout as a catalyst of both action and analysis.

text.text: Both traditions also share an affirmative vision of health. Ratner (2019) describes a joy that comes not from symptom relief, but from becoming fully alive, creatively confronting one's life, and openness to others.

text.text: Despite a reputation for resisting structure, existential therapy's core commitments appear to be widely shared, and outcome research suggests that existential-humanistic principles are integral to the effectiveness of bona fide psychotherapies (Angus et al., 2015; Elkins, 2009; Schneider & Längle, 2012).

text.text: The evidence reviewed here should be read with its limitations in mind.

Some are philosophical: existential therapists have historically doubted that there is a shared, objective reality that research instruments can measure, holding that experience can only be described phenomenologically (Vos, 2023), a stance that has no doubt contributed to a thinner evidence base than that of manualized approaches.

text.text: Moreover, the measures most often used, such as the PHQ-9 and GAD-7, capture exactly the outcomes existential therapy has regarded as secondary.
The approach is therefore evaluated on terms it does not fully accept.
Across this literature, existential therapy's strengths lie in treating dimensions of suffering that other approaches tend to bracket.

It takes seriously the distress that is not reducible to pathology, places the relationship at the center of care, and offers a framework of meaning that clients consistently describe as deeper than symptom relief.
Its commitments also appear to be clinically active: realness, presence, and meaning are related to alliance and outcome.

A further strength concerns empathy itself. Vanhooren (2022) distinguishes existential empathy from ontic empathy, which concerns the particulars of a client's daily struggles and in which the difference between self and other is easier to maintain.
text.formatted: A further strength concerns empathy itself. <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Vanhooren (2022)</ref> distinguishes existential empathy from ontic empathy, which concerns the particulars of a client's daily struggles and in which the difference between self and other is easier to maintain.

text.text: With existential struggles, the therapist must face the same givens as the client.
This makes existential empathy more demanding, but it also makes possible the "being-together" that existential therapists describe as central to their work.
Several limitations follow from this review's scope and method.
The review is narrative rather than systematic; sources were selected for theoretical and clinical relevance rather than through a structured search, so the synthesis is vulnerable to selection bias.

Some favorable findings may also reflect a survivorship effect: experienced existential therapists describe an early phase of discomfort with existential material that later gave way to growth and peace (Frediani et al., 2023), so studies that sample seasoned practitioners may understate how difficult the path is.

text.text: Other limitations are methodological.

The trials pooled by Vos and Vitali (2018) drew largely on patients with serious or life-threatening physical illness, which limits generalizability to broader outpatient settings, and the primary care data are uncontrolled. Vos and colleagues (2015) found weak or nonsignificant effects for non-meaning existential approaches (experiential-existential, supportive-expressive), consistent with meaning as an active ingredient, though structure, directiveness, and population are confounded with it.

text.text: Much of the support for existential processes is qualitative, drawn from small samples of clients and therapists who selfselected into existential work.

There is also a risk of partisanship: participants in existential training, even when not asked to compare, tend to judge other approaches as more superficial (Smith et al., 2023), which argues for an integrative approach to the philosophy of psychotherapy.

text.text: The comparison with CBT is instructive because the two approaches answer different questions.

CBT and other manualized approaches have become dominant partly because their structure makes them easy to measure, implement, and reimburse (Rayner & Vitali, 2016); that same structure is what existential therapy resists.
text.formatted: CBT and other manualized approaches have become dominant partly because their structure makes them easy to measure, implement, and reimburse <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Rayner & Vitali, 2016)</ref>; that same structure is what existential therapy resists.

text.text: The difference is sharpest around distortion.
Where CBT treats biased cognition as a target for correction, a phenomenological stance first asks whether a given perception is understandable in light of the person's circumstances (Ghaemi, 2007).
text.formatted: Where CBT treats biased cognition as a target for correction, a phenomenological stance first asks whether a given perception is understandable in light of the person's circumstances <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Ghaemi, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Existential therapy offers what CBT tends to set aside: the meaning of a symptom.
CBT offers what existential therapy has historically lacked: a transparent, testable account of what the therapist does and why.
The two are better seen as complements than as rivals.

Third-wave CBT therapists increasingly help clients live meaningful lives without fully adopting an existential framework (Vos, 2023), and the evidence reviewed here suggests that the relational and meaning-centered ingredients of existential therapy may strengthen structured treatments rather than compete with them.

text.text: The central challenge facing existential therapy is to become empirically legible without abandoning what makes it existential.

A recent scoping review of existential group psychotherapies notes that such groups have been applied across diagnoses and that standardized outcome measurement would strengthen the evidence base (Frøkedal et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A recent scoping review of existential group psychotherapies notes that such groups have been applied across diagnoses and that standardized outcome measurement would strengthen the evidence base <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Frøkedal et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Three directions follow from the present review: measuring existential therapy's proposed mechanisms, identifying for whom it works best, and training therapists to carry it out.

Existential therapy's proposed mechanisms (meaning, realness, presence, and existential empathy) can be measured (Geller et al., 2010; Hopwood et al., 2024; Steger et al., 2006; Vanhooren et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Existential therapy's proposed mechanisms (meaning, realness, presence, and existential empathy) can be measured <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Geller et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Hopwood et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Steger et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Vanhooren et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Research should track them as mechanisms of change rather than relying on pre-post symptom scales alone.
Even session-level questions, such as whether the client feels understood, accepted, and validated (Wharne, 2021), could anchor a measurement approach consistent with existential values.
text.formatted: Even session-level questions, such as whether the client feels understood, accepted, and validated <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Wharne, 2021)</ref>, could anchor a measurement approach consistent with existential values.

text.text: The desire to pick up this branch of therapeutic work is widespread, but the infrastructure is not well adapted to it.

Clinicians who work with meaning in life describe being held back by a lack of supervision, the perception that the approach is not evidence-based, training that ends at the undergraduate level, and the absence of guidance on bringing it into practice (Hill, 2017).

text.text: Existential empathy, moreover, depends on therapists' self-awareness of their own existential challenges, not only on knowledge of the ultimate concerns (Frediani et al., 2026; Vanhooren, 2022).

text.text: Training research should therefore examine how reflective practice and supervision can be structured so that trainees are not left alone with the profound uncertainty of existential training (Smith et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Training research should therefore examine how reflective practice and supervision can be structured so that trainees are not left alone with the profound uncertainty of existential training <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Smith et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Training should also draw on integrative models that combine existential principles with techniques from other modalities (Adams et al., 2025; Sotskova & Dossett, 2017), encouraging trainees to situate existential principles within empirical models rather than treat the two as opposing.

text.text: Rather than asking whether existential therapy works on average, research should ask for whom and under what conditions it works.
The finding that clients low on presence of meaning carry the greatest distress (Golovchanova et al., 2021) points to a subgroup for whom meaningcentered work may be especially indicated.

text.text: Idiographic designs, including intensive longitudinal and single-case methods, suit an approach that insists each client's situation is unique, because they model change within the person rather than averaging it away (Fisher et al., 2018; Molenaar, 2004).

text.text: Profile-or moderator-based matching could also give empirical form to existential therapy's longstanding emphasis on fit between client and therapist (Norcross & Wampold, 2011).

text.text: Treatment-selection models may appear to conflict with the commitment to clients as the authority over their experience.

The conflict dissolves when prediction is understood as informing rather than dictating: a model's estimate that a client is likely to benefit from meaning-centered work becomes one input to a decision the client and therapist make together.
Idiographic models go further, since they are built from the client's own session-bysession reports; while not a replacement of their account, it takes it seriously enough to measure.
Even the field's own meta-analysts have concluded that the pressing question is which existential intervention works best for which client (Vos et al., 2015).

text.text: Longitudinal Methods.
The most pressing open question is temporal: does change in meaning precede change in distress, follow it, or move alongside it?

Vos and Vitali's (2018) finding that increases in meaning predicted decreases in distress is consistent with meaning as a mechanism of change, but associations between pre-post scores cannot establish which change comes first.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Vos and Vitali's (2018)</ref> finding that increases in meaning predicted decreases in distress is consistent with meaning as a mechanism of change, but associations between pre-post scores cannot establish which change comes first.

text.text: Answering this requires repeated measurement across the course of treatment, which existential psychotherapy's empirical foundation currently lacks (Frøkedal et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Answering this requires repeated measurement across the course of treatment, which existential psychotherapy's empirical foundation currently lacks <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Frøkedal et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A feasible design would pair a brief client-reported measure of meaning, such as the Meaning in Life Questionnaire (Steger et al., 2006), and measures of the relational processes described above with standardized symptom measures (e.g., PHQ-9, GAD-7) administered each session.

text.text: Clinician ratings of client progress, collected alongside, would allow a direct comparison of how therapist and client each understand the unfolding work, a discrepancy with clinical consequences (Nakash et al., 2015).

text.text: In such a design, symptom scales are not the sole arbiter of success; they serve as a shared benchmark that allows comparison with other treatments.
Session-level data nested within clients call for multilevel modeling.
Mixed-effects models, linear or nonlinear, allow within-person effects to be separated from between-person effects (Curran & Bauer, 2011).

text.text: That clients with generally higher meaning report less distress is a between-person claim; that a given client's distress falls after their meaning rises is a within-person claim, and only the latter speaks to mechanism.

Lagged withinperson effects, in which meaning at one session predicts distress at the next while controlling for prior distress, supply the necessary temporal precedence that a mediation claim requires (Kazdin, 2007).

text.text: This directly tests whether clients low in meaning differ in the shape and magnitude of their benefit, and it moves toward treatment-selection models that estimate, for an individual, the expected advantage of one treatment over another.
Existential therapy's unique contribution is its insistence that suffering is not always a malfunction to be corrected.
Often it is a response to the conditions of existence, and it deserves to be understood.

Across the approach's philosophical foundations, core models, and emerging evidence base, the same commitments recur: meaning as a mechanism of recovery, the relationship as the site of change, and the client as the authority on their own experience.
These commitments are not relics.

Meaning-centered interventions promote quality of life while reducing distress, therapeutic realness tracks the alliance, and existential-humanistic principles appear integral to effective psychotherapy broadly.

What existential therapy lacks is not relevance but infrastructure: measurement that captures its mechanisms, methods that identify whom it serves best, and training that prepares therapists to meet existential encounters rather than withdraw from them. Wharne (2021) suggests the scientist-practitioner might take an agnostic stance toward the client's world, not knowing whether the room is bugged or the client unjustly paranoid until evidence settles the question.

text.text: Existential therapy asks for more than agnosticism: that the therapist genuinely entertain the possibility that the client's way of seeing is justified, and in doing so, learn a perspective that formality would otherwise miss.
Existentialism's place in psychotherapy is not a lost art to be recovered from history.
It is a set of commitments the field already depends on.
The end goal is to make them visible, precise, and teachable.
